derivations.claim: For every $s$, [F4] with $V=1$ gives $\mathbb E|X(s)|\le(\mathbb E[X(s)^2])^{1/2}=M<\infty$, where $M$ is constant by the stated first- and second-order stationarity. The map $(s,\omega)\mapsto |X(s,\omega)|$ is product-measurable; Tonelli [F5] gives $\mathbb E\int_{W_n}|X(s)|\,ds =\int_{W_n}\mathbb E|X(s)|\,ds\le M|W_n|<\infty.$ Therefore the sample path is absolutely integrable almost surely. Tonelli also makes the event where this integral is finite measurable; its probability is one. Applying Tonelli separately to $X^+$ and $X^-$ makes both section integrals measurable, and their difference on that event, extended by zero on its null complement as in [A2], is measurable.

Since $\int_{W_n}\mathbb E|X(s)|\,ds<\infty$, Fubini [F6] applies to $X$ on $W_n\times\Omega$. Its constant mean gives $\mathbb E[\bar X_{W_n}]=\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}\mathbb E[X(s)]\,ds =\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}\mu\,ds=\mu.$

Put $Z(s):=X(s)-\mu$. By [F4], $\mathbb E|Z(s)Z(t)|\le C(0)$ for all $s,t$, so this pair-product is integrable on $W_n\times W_n\times\Omega$ because $|W_n|<\infty$. Fubini [F6] and the covariance definition [F2] yield $\mathbb E\bigl[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2\bigr] =\frac1{|W_n|^2}\int_{W_n}\int_{W_n}C(t-s)\,dt\,ds.$ This also proves $\bar X_{W_n}\in L^2$.

Define $q_n(h):=|W_n\cap(W_n-h)|/|W_n|$. It is measurable by the section-integral measurability in [F5] applied to $\mathbf1_{W_n}(s)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)$, and $0\le q_n(h)\le1$. For fixed $h$, translation invariance [F7] gives $|W_n\setminus(W_n-h)|=|(W_n+h)\setminus W_n|.$ The latter is bounded by $|(W_n+\{0,h\})\setminus W_n|$, so the Van Hove condition [A1] implies $q_n(h)\to1$.

The integrand is absolutely integrable, since for each $s$ its absolute integral over $t\in W_n$ is at most $\|C\|_1$. In the inner integral set $h=t-s$; translation invariance [F7] gives $\mathbb E\bigl[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2\bigr] =\frac1{|W_n|^2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)|W_n\cap(W_n-h)|\,dh.$ The overlap factor is the measure of those $s\in W_n$ for which $s+h\in W_n$.

Multiplying the formula in step 2.1 by $|W_n|$ gives $|W_n|\,\mathbb E[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2]=\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)q_n(h)\,dh.$ By [F10], the right side converges to $\int C(h)\,dh$ because $|C(h)q_n(h)|\le|C(h)|\in L^1$. It is therefore bounded; since $|W_n|\to\infty$, step 2.1 implies $\mathbb E[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2]\to0$.
The mean identity in step 1.2 and the second-moment limit in step 3.1 are exactly $L^2$ convergence to $\mu$ by [F8].

derivations.claim: The additive group of $\mathbb Z$ is abelian by [F1]. Coordinatewise addition on $\mathbb Z^d$ is associative and commutative, has the zero vector as identity, and sends $x$ to $-x$ coordinatewise as its inverse. Hence $\mathbb Z^d$ is an abelian group.

For distinct $x,y\in\mathbb Z^d$, the singleton sets $\{x\}$ and $\{y\}$ are disjoint open neighbourhoods by [F2], so the space is Hausdorff by [F6]. Each singleton $\{x\}$ is finite and hence compact by [F7]; it is an open neighbourhood of $x$ by [F2]. Thus the space is locally compact by [F8].

The product topology on $\mathbb Z^d\times\mathbb Z^d$ is discrete: for each pair $(x,y)$, the basic open set $\{x\}\times\{y\}$ is its singleton by [F2, F3]. Therefore coordinatewise addition $\mathbb Z^d\times\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb Z^d$ and inversion $\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb Z^d$ are continuous by [F4]. By [F5] the group is a topological group, and with step 1.2 it is locally compact Hausdorff abelian. Every map from $\mathbb Z^d$ is continuous by [F2, F4].

derivations.claim: For $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\in\mathbb T^d$, the formula for $\Psi(z)$ is a homomorphism because for $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z^d$, $\Psi(z)(k+\ell)=\prod_r z_r^{k_r+\ell_r} =\left(\prod_r z_r^{k_r}\right)\left(\prod_r z_r^{\ell_r}\right).$ It is continuous because its domain $\mathbb Z^d$ is discrete, so every preimage of an open set is open. Therefore $\Psi(z)\in\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$.

The map $\Psi$ is a group homomorphism because $\Psi(zz')(k)=\prod_r(z_rz'_r)^{k_r} =\left(\prod_rz_r^{k_r}\right)\left(\prod_r(z'_r)^{k_r}\right)$ by [F3] and commutativity of $\mathbb T$ [F4]. If $\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$, put $z_r:=\chi(e_r)$, where $e_r$ is the $r$th standard basis vector. Then $z_r\in\mathbb T$ by [F1], and the decomposition $k=\sum_r k_re_r$ together with homomorphism and power laws gives $\chi(k)=\prod_r z_r^{k_r}$. Thus $\chi=\Psi(z)$; also $z_r=\chi(e_r)$ recovers each coordinate uniquely, so $\Psi$ is bijective.

For each fixed $k$, the coordinate map $z\mapsto\Psi(z)(k)$ is a finite product of continuous integer-power maps on $\mathbb T$, hence continuous by [F4]. The product-topology criterion and [F2] then imply that $\Psi$ is continuous into $\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$.

The inverse map is $\chi\mapsto(\chi(e_1),\ldots,\chi(e_d))$. Each coordinate is continuous by [F2], so the inverse is continuous into the finite product $\mathbb T^d$. Thus $\Psi$ is a homeomorphism by [F5] and a group isomorphism by step 1.2 and the pointwise group law in [F1].

derivations.claim: If $B_1,B_2,\ldots$ are pairwise disjoint Borel subsets of $\mathbb T^d$, then their images under the bijection $\Psi$ are pairwise disjoint Borel sets by [F1]. Hence $F\!\left(\bigcup_{m\ge1}B_m\right) =\mu\!\left(\bigcup_{m\ge1}\Psi(B_m)\right) =\sum_{m\ge1}\mu(\Psi(B_m)) =\sum_{m\ge1}F(B_m).$ Thus $F$ is a positive measure, and $F(\mathbb T^d)=\mu(\widehat{\mathbb Z^d})<\infty$.

For Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb T^d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, outer regularity of $\mu$ gives an open $U\supseteq\Psi(B)$ with $\mu(U)<\mu(\Psi(B))+\varepsilon$. Then $\Psi^{-1}(U)$ is open, contains $B$, and $F(\Psi^{-1}(U))=\mu(U)$, proving outer regularity of $F$. If $U$ is open in $\mathbb T^d$, inner regularity of $\mu$ gives compact $C\subseteq\Psi(U)$ with $\mu(C)>\mu(\Psi(U))-\varepsilon$. Then $\Psi^{-1}(C)$ is compact in $U$ and $F(\Psi^{-1}(C))=\mu(C)$, proving inner regularity on open sets. The torus is compact Hausdorff by [F4], so these properties make $F$ Radon as in [F2].

For an indicator $g=\mathbf1_B$ of a Borel set, $\int g\,dF=F(B)=\mu(\Psi(B)) =\int \mathbf1_B(\Psi^{-1}(\chi))\,\mu(d\chi).$ Finite linearity [F3] extends this equality to Borel simple functions. For a nonnegative Borel function, choose increasing simple approximations and apply monotone convergence [F3] on both spaces. Splitting the real and imaginary parts of a bounded complex Borel function into positive and negative parts then gives the asserted integral identity by [F5].

Expanding its squared modulus, using [F6] and stationarity, gives $\sum_{r,s}a_r\overline{a_s}c(k_r-k_s) =\mathbb E\left|\sum_r a_r(Y_{k_r}-\mu)\right|^2\ge0.$ Thus $c$ is positive definite by [F1].

By [F9], $\mathbb Z^d$ is a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group and every function on it is continuous, so $c$ is continuous. By Bochner's theorem [F2], using AC [A1] and DC [A2], there is a unique finite positive Radon measure $F_0$ on $\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$ such that $c(h)=\int_{\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}}\chi(h)\,F_0(d\chi).$

Expand the finite squared modulus in [F5]. Every product is integrable by [F7], and stationarity gives $\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\frac1{(2\pi)^dn^d}\sum_{j,k\in\Lambda_n} c(j-k)e^{-i(j-k)\cdot\lambda}.$

By [F3] and [F4], transport $F_0$ to the unique finite positive Radon measure $F$ on $\mathbb T^d$. Applying the integral-transport identity [F4] to $\chi\mapsto\chi(h)$ gives $c(h)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}e^{ih\cdot\theta}\,F(d\theta).$

Substitute the spectral representation from step 2.1 into each summand of step 1.3. Linearity permits moving the finite sum through the integral, and $\sum_{j,k\in\Lambda_n}e^{-i(j-k)\cdot(\lambda-\theta)} =\left|\sum_{j\in\Lambda_n}e^{-ij\cdot(\lambda-\theta)}\right|^2.$ After dividing by $(2\pi)^dn^d$ this is precisely $\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)\,F(d\theta).$

The displayed kernel factors into nonnegative one-dimensional kernels. For each coordinate, expanding the finite square and applying angular orthogonality [F10] to each integer exponent $a-b$ gives $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac1{2\pi n} \left|\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}e^{-iax}\right|^2dx=1.$ The Countable Choice hypothesis of [F10] follows from AC by [F11] and [A1]. Fubini [F8] for the finite product then gives $\int_{\mathbb T^d}\Phi_n(x)\,dx=1,$ and nonnegativity follows from the squared modulus.

derivations.claim: Write $\phi_n(x):=(2\pi n)^{-1}|\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}e^{-iax}|^2$, so $\Phi_n(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d\phi_n(x_r)$ by [F1]. Fix $0<\delta<\pi$. If the circular distance of $x$ from $0$ is at least $\delta$, choose its representative in $[-\pi,\pi]$; then $|\sin(x/2)|\ge\sin(\delta/2)>0$ by [F2]. The finite geometric-series formula therefore gives $\phi_n(x)=\frac1{2\pi n} \left|\frac{\sin(nx/2)}{\sin(x/2)}\right|^2 \le\frac1{2\pi n\sin^2(\delta/2)}.$ By the union bound over coordinates and the unit integral of each factor from [F1], $\int_{\{x:\rho_\infty(x,0)\ge\delta\}}\Phi_n(x)\,dx \le\frac{d}{n\sin^2(\delta/2)},$ where $\rho_\infty$ is the maximum circular distance over the $d$ coordinates.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Continuity of $f$ at $\lambda_0$ gives $0<\delta<\pi$ such that $|f(\theta)-f(\lambda_0)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $\rho_\infty(\theta,\lambda_0)<2\delta$. For any $\lambda'$ with $\rho_\infty(\lambda',\lambda_0)<\delta$, split the convolution in [F1] into that neighborhood and its complement. On the neighborhood its contribution to $|g_n(\lambda')-f(\lambda_0)|$ is at most $\varepsilon$ because $\Phi_n$ has integral one. On the complement, $\rho_\infty(\lambda'-\theta,0)\ge\delta$; with $M:=\|f\|_\infty+|f(\lambda_0)|<\infty$, step 1.1 gives $|g_n(\lambda')-f(\lambda_0)| \le\varepsilon+\frac{Md}{n\sin^2(\delta/2)}.$ This bound holds uniformly for all such $\lambda'$.

Since $K$ is continuous and $K(0)>0$, there is $a>0$ such that $K(u)>0$ whenever $\|u\|_\infty<a$. A nearest Fourier-grid point to $\lambda_0$ is within $\pi/n$ in each circular coordinate. Since $n b_n\to\infty$, eventually $\pi/(n b_n)<a$, so the periodized kernel is positive at that grid point and the denominator in [A1] is positive. Moreover, if a weight in [A1] is positive, compact support of $K$ implies its grid point is within circular distance $R b_n$ of $\lambda_0$ in every coordinate, where $[-R,R]^d$ contains the support of $K$. Since $b_n\to0$, all positive-weight grid points eventually lie within the $\delta$-neighborhood from step 2.1.

For all sufficiently large $n$, [F3] and [A1] give $\mathbb E[\widetilde f_{n,b_n}(\lambda_0)] =\sum_{q\in\Lambda_n}w_{n,q,b_n}(\lambda_0) g_n(\lambda_{n,q}).$ The weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and every positive weight is on a grid point covered by step 2.1. Hence $\left|\mathbb E[\widetilde f_{n,b_n}(\lambda_0)]-f(\lambda_0)\right| \le\varepsilon+\frac{Md}{n\sin^2(\delta/2)}.$ Taking $n\to\infty$ and then arbitrary $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the claimed bias limit.

derivations.claim: Take the data $(y_0,y_1,y_2)=(1,2,3)$ on $V=\{0,1,2\}$. Its mean is $\bar y=2$. By [F1], the lag-zero estimator is $\widehat C(0)=\frac{1^2+2^2+3^2}{3}-2^2=\frac23,$ and the lag-two estimate, based on the single pair $(0,2)$, is $\widehat C(2)=1\cdot3-2^2=-1.$ The negative-lag estimate equals $\widehat C(-2)=\widehat C(2)$ because the reverse pair has the same product.

At the two sites $0$ and $2$, all pairwise lag estimates are defined and the estimated covariance matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2/3&-1\\-1&2/3\end{pmatrix}.$ Its quadratic form at $v=(1,1)^T$ equals $v^T\begin{pmatrix}2/3&-1\\-1&2/3\end{pmatrix}v=-2/3<0$. This contradicts the necessary nonnegative quadratic-form condition [F2], so the stated universal claim is false.
